subject: physics
question_text: Can the coefficient of friction be greater than one?

verification.note: Sri Chaitanya IPE Junior Fastrack (Rev. May 2024), Unit 5 VERY SHORT ANSWER. The 1+1 mark split is invented and needs a Telangana IPE teacher; no exam appearance years are printed for this question, so appearances[] stays empty.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The answer

lines.text: Yes, μ can be greater than one.

lines: For most pairs of surfaces it is less
than one, but that is not a rule.
steps.margin_note: Answer yes in the first line. A hedged opening loses the mark.
steps.why: μ is only the ratio f/N that a particular pair of surfaces happens to give. Nothing in the definition caps it at one.
common_mistakes: Answering "no" because every textbook example happens to be below one.

recall.must_convey: That yes, the coefficient of friction can be greater than one.
accept: yes it can be greater than one
yes more than one is possible

steps.memory_tip: Yes — μ is a measured ratio f/N, and nothing in the definition caps it at 1.

steps.label: The reason
lines: When two surfaces are highly polished,
the molecules come very close and
f can exceed N, so μ = f/N is above 1.
steps.margin_note: Finish on μ = f/N. The ratio is what makes "greater than one" mean anything.
steps.why: The board wants the adhesion reason. The honest general statement is broader: μ is a measured ratio, and pairs such as rubber on rubber pass 1 with no polishing at all.
common_mistakes: Saying polishing always REDUCES friction. Past a point, very smooth surfaces stick.

recall.must_convey: That highly polished surfaces increase adhesion, so friction can exceed the normal force.
accept: friction becomes more than normal force
mu is f by N so it can cross one
reject: yes it can be greater than one

steps.memory_tip: Give the board reason: highly polished surfaces stick by adhesion, which pushes f above N.

insider_note: A plain yes on the first line, the adhesion reason on the second. An opening that only says most surfaces are below one loses the first mark.
